edits.find:
When a stem describes an illness and says the patient "remains on medication" without naming it, the question is a two-step inference: identify the drug class the illness requires, then choose the member whose side-effect profile matches the complaint. Psychosis → antipsychotic → the one with the highest prolactin liability.

The number is the discriminator. Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia runs 25–100 and rarely exceeds 200; a prolactinoma typically produces >200. A level of 70 assassinates the prolactinoma option without any imaging.
edits.with:

Then choose the member of that class whose side-effect profile matches the complaint. For psychosis, choose the antipsychotic with the highest prolactin liability.

The prolactin level separates the causes. Drug-induced hyperprolactinemia runs 25–100 and rarely exceeds 200, while a prolactinoma typically produces >200. A level of 70 excludes prolactinoma without any imaging.

edits.find:
DXA at age 65 for all women — or earlier if she has ≥1 risk factor (prior fragility fracture, parental hip fracture, smoking, low BMI, chronic glucocorticoids). Run the risk-factor list before applying the age default. A patient with timely menopause and an empty list waits until 65.

⚠︎ Two ledgers. The rule above is the exam ledger and the operational shorthand. The USPSTF statement expresses the same idea quantitatively: screen before 65 when a FRAX-estimated 10-year major osteoporotic fracture risk reaches that of a 65-year-old with no risk factors (~9.3%). The exam scores the risk-factor list; know FRAX for the clinic and for questions that hand you a percentage. Fully worked in the board-style brief DEXA: When Screening Starts Early.

The most common time-waster here: obesity is protective for osteoporosis, not a risk factor. The risk factor is low body weight (<58 kg / 127 lb) — higher weight increases bone density through mechanical loading and peripheral aromatization to estrogen.

Screen earlier if she has ≥1 risk factor: prior fragility fracture, parental hip fracture, smoking, low BMI (body mass index) or chronic glucocorticoids. Run the risk-factor list before applying the age default. A patient with timely menopause and no risk factors waits until 65.

⚠︎ Exam answer versus clinical practice. The rule above is the exam answer and the operational shorthand. The USPSTF (US Preventive Services Task Force) statement expresses the same idea quantitatively, using FRAX (Fracture Risk Assessment Tool). Screen before 65 when the FRAX-estimated 10-year major osteoporotic fracture risk reaches that of a 65-year-old with no risk factors (~9.3%). The exam scores the risk-factor list. Use FRAX in clinical practice and when a question gives a percentage. The board-style brief DEXA: When Screening Starts Early works this through in full.

Obesity is protective for osteoporosis, not a risk factor. The risk factor is low body weight (<58 kg / 127 lb). Higher weight increases bone density through mechanical loading and peripheral aromatization to estrogen.
